title: Light: Reflection and Refraction
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Physics
summary: How a ray of light changes direction when it reflects from a plane mirror (angle of incidence = angle of reflection) and when it passes from one medium into another (refraction).

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Describe how a ray of light **changes direction when it reflects** from a flat (plane) mirror (6Ps.01).
Describe how a ray of light **changes direction when it passes from one material into another** (for example from air into water or glass), and know that this is called **refraction** (6Ps.02).

blocks.text: 1. Light travels in straight lines

Light comes from **light sources** such as the Sun, a lamp, a torch or a flame. Light travels in **straight lines**. We show the path of light with a **ray**: a straight line drawn with a ruler, with an **arrow** showing which way the light is going.

Most things around you are not light sources. You see a book because light from a source **reflects** (bounces) off the book and travels into your **eyes**. So in any diagram about seeing, the arrows must point **from** the source, **to** the object, and **into** the eye — never out of the eye.

blocks.text: 2. Reflection from a plane mirror

When a ray of light hits a plane mirror it **changes direction** and bounces off. A plane mirror is very smooth, so it reflects light in a neat, predictable way. To describe the direction we draw the **normal**: a dashed line at **90°** to the mirror at the point where the ray hits. Then we measure both angles **from the normal**.

blocks.title: The law of reflection
blocks.text: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the normal. The incident ray and the reflected ray are on **opposite sides** of the normal.

items: A ray that hits the mirror along the normal (angle of incidence 0°) reflects straight back the way it came.
A ray with a bigger angle of incidence gives an equally bigger angle of reflection: 20° → 20°, 55° → 55°.

Smooth, shiny surfaces (mirrors, still water, polished metal) reflect light **regularly**, so you see a clear image. Rough surfaces (paper, cloth) scatter the light in all directions, so no image forms — but you can still see the paper because some of that scattered light reaches your eye.

blocks.text: **How to draw a reflected ray — step by step**

items: Mark the point where the incident ray meets the mirror.
Draw the normal with a ruler and protractor: a dashed line at 90° to the mirror through that point.
Measure the angle of incidence between the incident ray and the **normal** (not the mirror).
On the other side of the normal, measure the same angle and draw the reflected ray with a ruler.
Add arrows: towards the mirror on the incident ray, away from the mirror on the reflected ray.

blocks.title: Trap: the angle to the mirror
blocks.text: If a question gives the angle between the ray and the **mirror surface**, subtract it from 90° first. A ray at 70° to the mirror has an angle of incidence of 90° − 70° = **20°**, so the angle of reflection is 20°.
3. Using mirrors: the periscope and mirror images

A **periscope** lets you see over a wall or out of a submarine. It is a tube with two plane mirrors, each at **45°**. Light from the object hits the top mirror and is reflected **down** the tube (it turns through 90°). It then hits the bottom mirror and is reflected through 90° again, out into your eye.

blocks.text: Your **image** in a plane mirror is the same size as you, the same distance behind the mirror as you are in front, the right way up, but **reversed left to right**: lift your right hand and the image lifts its left hand. This is why some ambulances have the word AMBULANCE written backwards on the front — drivers in front read it the right way round in their mirrors.
4. Refraction: light bending between media

Light travels at different speeds in different media: fastest in air, slower in water, slower still in glass. When a ray passes from one transparent medium into another **at an angle**, the change of speed makes it **change direction** at the boundary. This bending is called **refraction**.

blocks.text: Refraction explains many everyday things:

items: A straw in a glass of water looks **bent** or broken at the water surface.
A swimming pool or a pond looks **shallower** than it really is — be careful before jumping in.
Your legs look shorter when you stand in a pool.
**Lenses** in glasses, magnifying glasses, cameras and microscopes are shaped so that refraction bends the light to make clear or bigger images.
The "coin trick" below.

blocks.title: بالعربي — الفرق بين الانعكاس والانكسار
items: الانعكاس (reflection): الضوء يخبط في المراية ويرجع. القاعدة: زاوية السقوط = زاوية الانعكاس، والزاويتين بتتقاسوا من العمود (normal) مش من المراية.
لو الزاوية مدياها مع المراية نفسها، اطرحها من 90° الأول.
الانكسار (refraction): الضوء يعدّي من وسط لوسط (هوا ← مية أو زجاج) فيتكسر ويغير اتجاهه لأن سرعته بتتغير.
داخل للزجاج أو المية: يقرّب من العمود. خارج للهوا: يبعد عن العمود. لو داخل على العمود بالظبط: يكمل مستقيم.

blocks.text: 6. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle of incidence is 35°. (a) What is the angle of reflection? [1] (b) What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray? [1]
**Answer:** (a) **35°** (angle of incidence = angle of reflection). (b) Both angles are measured from the normal on opposite sides, so the total is 35° + 35° = **70°**.
**Worked example 2** — A ray makes an angle of 60° with the surface of a mirror. Work out the angle of reflection. Show your working. [2]

blocks.caption: The 60° is measured between the ray and the mirror, not the normal.

blocks.text: **Working:** angle of incidence = 90° − 60° = 30° (1 mark). Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = **30°** (1 mark). **Common mistake:** answering 60° — that angle is measured from the mirror, not the normal.
**Worked example 3** — Explain how a periscope lets Karim see a football match over a high wall. [2]

**Answer:** Light from the match hits the **top mirror** and is **reflected down** the tube (1 mark). It is then reflected by the **bottom mirror**, out of the tube into Karim's **eye** (1 mark). (Extra detail that shows understanding: the mirrors are at 45°, so each turns the light through 90°.)
**Worked example 4** — A ray of light travels from air into a glass block at an angle. Ring the correct word in each sentence. [2]

items: The ray bends **towards** / away from the normal as it enters the glass. → **towards** (it slows down).
The ray bends towards / **away from** the normal as it leaves the glass into the air. → **away from** (it speeds up).
What is the name of this bending of light? → **refraction**.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — Explain why a coin at the bottom of a cup appears when water is poured in. [2]

**Answer:** Light from the coin is **refracted** (bends) when it passes from the **water into the air** (1 mark). It bends away from the normal, so it passes over the rim of the cup and **reaches the eye** (1 mark). **Common mistake:** saying the coin "floats up" — the coin does not move, only the light changes direction.
**Worked example 6 (investigation)** — Hana shines a ray from a ray box at a plane mirror and measures the angles with a protractor.

items: (a) Describe the pattern. [1] → The angle of reflection is (about) **equal to** the angle of incidence.
(b) Which result is anomalous? [1] → **45° (for 60°)** — it should be about 60°.
(c) Suggest why 31° and 49° are not exactly 30° and 50°. [1] → small errors in drawing the ray or reading the protractor (the ray is quite wide).
(d) How could Hana make her results more reliable? [1] → **repeat** each measurement and use a narrow ray / sharp pencil; repeat the anomalous one.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Measuring angles from the **mirror** or the glass surface instead of from the **normal**.
Drawing rays with no arrows, or with arrows coming **out of** the eye.
Drawing rays freehand — always use a ruler; light travels in straight lines.
Mixing up the words: reflection = bounces off; **refraction** = bends as it passes into a new medium.
Saying a ray that enters glass along the normal is bent — at 90° to the surface it goes straight on.
Getting "towards" and "away from" the normal the wrong way round. Into glass or water: towards. Out into air: away.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Complete the ray diagram:** draw the reflected ray with a ruler and protractor; add the normal and arrows.
**Give the angle:** angle of reflection, the angle between the two rays, or the angle from a ray to the mirror (watch for the 90° trap).
**Ring the correct word / complete the sentence:** towards / away from the normal; reflection / refraction.
**Explain an everyday effect:** bent straw, shallow pool, coin trick, periscope — name the process and say where the light changes direction.
**Investigation with a ray box:** describe the pattern in a results table, spot the anomalous angle, suggest improvements (repeat, use a narrow ray).

questions.e: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 25°.

questions.q: What is the angle of reflection?
questions.e: Angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90° − 60° = 30°. So the angle of reflection = 30°.

questions.q: What is the name of the line drawn at 90° to a mirror where a ray hits it?
questions.e: The normal is the imaginary line at right angles (90°) to the surface; angles are measured from it.

questions.q: Complete the sentence with one word: When light passes from air into water and changes direction, this is called ______.
questions.e: The bending of light as it passes from one medium into another is refraction.

questions.q: Which line shows the reflected ray?
questions.e: The reflected ray must be on the other side of the normal at the same angle as the incident ray: 30°. That is B. A is at 60° and C at only 10° from the normal; D goes through the mirror, which light cannot do.

questions.q: A ray of light enters a glass block **along the normal** (at 90° to the surface). What happens to it?
c: It bends away from the normal.
It goes straight on without changing direction.
questions.e: A ray along the normal does not change direction when it enters the glass (it only slows down).

questions.q: A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface. Why?
c: Light is refracted as it passes from the water into the air.
Light is reflected by the pencil.
Light travels faster in water than in air.
questions.e: Light from the part of the pencil under water changes direction (refracts) at the water surface, so that part appears in a different place.

questions.q: A ray hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 40°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
questions.e: Angle of reflection = 40°. The two rays are on opposite sides of the normal, so the angle between them = 40° + 40° = 80°.

questions.q: In a periscope, each mirror is fixed at an angle to the tube. What is this angle, in degrees?
questions.e: The mirrors are at 45°, so each one turns the light through 90°.

questions.q: A ray of light passes from glass into air at an angle. Which way does it bend?
c: it always reflects back into the glass
questions.e: Going from glass into air, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.q: Which surface would give the clearest reflection (image)?
questions.e: Smooth, shiny, flat surfaces reflect light regularly, so they form a clear image. Rough surfaces scatter the light.

questions.q: Explain how a periscope helps you to see over a wall. Use the word reflect in your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: light (from the object) is reflected by the top mirror down the tube. 1 mark: it is reflected again by the bottom mirror into the eye. Accept: each mirror at 45° turns the light through 90°. Do not accept rays going out of the eye.
questions.e: Light from the object hits the top mirror and is reflected down the tube; the bottom mirror reflects it again into your eye.

questions.q: Ahmed looks into a clear swimming pool. The pool looks shallower than it really is. Name the process that causes this and say where the light changes direction. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: refraction. 1 mark: at the water surface / as light passes from the water into the air (it bends away from the normal). Do not accept reflection.
questions.e: Refraction. Light from the bottom of the pool bends at the surface as it leaves the water and enters the air, so the bottom appears higher (nearer) than it really is.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Light travels in straight lines; draw rays with a ruler and arrows.
Plane mirror: **angle of incidence = angle of reflection**, both measured from the **normal**.
Angle given to the mirror? Subtract from 90° first.
**Refraction** = light changing direction as it passes from one medium to another (air, water, glass).
Into glass/water: bends **towards** the normal. Out into air: bends **away from** the normal. Along the normal: no bend.
Uses and effects: periscope (two 45° mirrors), bent straw, shallow-looking pool, lenses.
